title: The face reader's answer
translation: Myōun, the head priest of Mount Hiei, once went to see a man who read faces. "Is there any danger that I'll die by a weapon?" he asked.
"You're a man who should have nothing to fear from weapons. And yet the thought came to you, and you asked. That alone is the sign of the danger."
And sure enough, he was killed by an arrow.
original: {明雲|めいうん}{座主|ざす}、{相者|さうじや}に{逢|あ}ひ{給|たま}ひて、「{己|おのれ}{若|も}し{兵仗|ひやうぢやう}の{難|なん}やある。」と{尋|たづ}ねたまひければ、
{相人|さうにん}、「{実|まこと}にその{相|さう}おはします。」と{申|まう}す。
「いかなる{相|さう}ぞ。」と{尋|たづ}ね{給|たま}ひければ、
「{傷害|しやうがい}の{恐|おそ}れおはしますまじき{御身|おんみ}にて、{仮|かり}にもかく{思|おぼ}しよりて{尋|たづ}ね{給|たま}ふ。これ{既|すで}にそのあやぶみの{兆|きざし}なり。」と{申|まう}しけり。
はたして{矢|や}にあたりてうせ{給|たま}ひにけり。
literal: The abbot Myōun met a physiognomist and asked, 'Is there perhaps a danger of weapons for me?', and
the physiognomist said, 'Truly, you have that sign.'
When he asked, 'What kind of sign is it?',
(the physiognomist) said: 'Being a person who should have no fear of injury, you even so much as thought of this and asked. This is already the omen of that danger.'
Sure enough, he was struck by an arrow and died.

notes.text: Myōun (1115–1184), twice head ({座主|ざす}) of the Tendai school at Enryakuji on Mount Hiei, the great monastery north-east of Kyoto. He was killed when Kiso Yoshinaka's troops attacked Retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa's Hōjūji palace at the end of 1183 by the Japanese calendar.

{相者|さうじや}, also {相人|さうにん}: a physiognomist, someone who tells fortunes from a person's face and body ({相|さう}, as in section 145). The two sections are a pair: in both, an expert reads a sign, and in both the sign turns out to be a plain observation.
{兵仗|ひやうぢやう}: weapons. {難|なん}: a disaster. The 1925 edition: the sign of dying by a weapon.

notes.quote: 傷害の恐れおはしますまじき御身にて
notes.text: まじ: 'should not'. A high priest has no reason to fear weapons. おはします: the face reader speaks to him with high respect.

notes.quote: これ既にそのあやぶみの兆なり
notes.text: The answer is a clever turn: asking the question is itself the omen. The text does not say whether the face reader saw more than that.
はたして: 'sure enough, as predicted'. Modern Japanese still has the word.
